title: Constantine
hookLine: an emperor sees a sign before battle, and everything changes for the church, for good and ill

lines: ON THE WRONG SIDE OF POWER.
cards: For days now, the people in this story have been on the wrong side of power: a letter explaining Christians to outsiders, Justin writing to the emperor, Perpetua in the arena, Tertullian daring the governors, Cyprian's people nursing the sick.

Today the camera turns around. A Roman ruler named Constantine is marching on Rome to fight a rival for the empire, and before the battle, by his own account, he sees something in the sky. He is not a Christian.
He's about to become a very powerful friend to the church, and that changes the story.

teach.b: Two old accounts survive, and they don't match exactly.
Eusebius, a bishop who knew Constantine, writes that the emperor told him, and swore to it, that around noon he saw a cross of light above the sun, with words: by this, conquer.

That night, Eusebius says, Christ appeared to him in a dream and told him to copy the sign and carry it into battle. So Constantine had a standard made with the first two Greek letters of Christ's name.
Lactantius, another writer of the time, tells it more simply: in a dream, Constantine was told to mark the heavenly sign of God on his soldiers' shields, and he did.

teach.h: TWO ACCOUNTS: A VISION, A DREAM.
teach.b: A vision, a dream, or both; the sources differ.
What happened next: Constantine won, and he favored the church. Christians who had been hunted found their emperor on their side. Their buildings could rise in public.

Their bishops could meet openly. And the other side: when the emperor is your friend, the emperor has opinions about your church. Faith and power start to tangle in ways Christians have argued about since.

teach.h: MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.
teach.b: Jesus had said, "My kingdom is not of this world." Now a kingdom of this world carried his sign into battle. Christians still weigh this differently.

Some see Constantine as God's answer to the prayers of the persecuted, and the Orthodox Church honors him as a saint. Others see the moment the church began to trade the arena for the palace, and wonder what it cost.
Some hold both. One more detail from Eusebius: Constantine was baptized only near the end of his life.

how: The Orthodox Church honors Constantine as a saint, together with his mother Helena; other Christians remember him as a pivotal and debated figure in the church's history with the state.

o: a bishop who saw a cross of light above the sun
the emperor who turned the church from hunted to favored
the emperor who first hunted Christians in the arena

games.q: the two accounts — tap the pairs.
p: a cross of light above the sun
a dream: a sign on the shields
My kingdom is not of this world

s: the old sources agree exactly on what Constantine saw
Eusebius tells of a cross of light in the sky and a dream; Lactantius tells only of a dream.
Eusebius says Constantine was baptized only near the end of his life
he favored the church long before he was baptized.
the Latin words in hoc signo vinces are what Eusebius wrote
Eusebius wrote in Greek: touto nika, by this conquer. the Latin form is a later wording.

games.q: you're a bishop. the emperor who once would have killed you now wants to be your friend, build your churches and attend your meetings. what do you do?
o: welcome it: the persecution is over.
refuse: the church must stay away from power.
welcome it, and worry about what it will cost.
games.why: the church welcomed Constantine's favor, and Christians still argue about what it cost. both the relief and the worry are part of the story.

practice: Bring to mind one place where you hold a little power: at work, at home, in a group, over someone newer than you. Ask what your beliefs, about God or about people, ask of you there, and where the power might be shaping the belief.
If you pray, bring that place before God; if not, look at it honestly for this minute.

wordCard.voice: Constantine. The emperor who said he saw a sign before battle, and who turned the church from hunted to favored, for good and ill.

orig.note: Greek: by this, conquer. the words Eusebius says Constantine saw with the sign.

carryVoice: Your line: power changes things. For good, and for ill, and Christians still argue which. See you tomorrow.
